target.title: fix(openai): bound image generation SSE body reads with idle timeout
target.body:
## Summary
Add idle-timeout protection to OpenAI Codex image generation SSE response body reads so stalled response bodies fail with a bounded deadline instead of hanging indefinitely after response headers arrive.

## What Problem This Solves
OpenAI Codex image generation could hang indefinitely when the API returned response headers but then stalled while streaming the SSE response body.

- The `readResponseBodyText` function reads the response body with a bare `reader.read()` in a loop — no idle timeout on individual chunk reads.
- If the server stops producing chunks mid-stream, the reader waits forever.
- The fetch-level timeout covers response headers, but once headers arrive the body read is unbounded.

**Code evidence**: In `extensions/openai/image-generation-provider.ts:528`, the `reader.read()` call lacks any idle deadline, unlike the shared `readChunkWithIdleTimeout` utility in `src/infra/http-body.ts` which is already used by Signal, media-core, and other paths.

## Root Cause
- The `readResponseBodyText` function was written before `readChunkWithIdleTimeout` became the standard pattern for bounded body reads.
- The utility was not re-exported from `src/plugin-sdk/media-runtime.ts` barrel, so extension code couldn't import it.
- Other extensions (Signal in #104122, Telegram in #106035) have since adopted idle-timeout body readers.
- The OpenAI image generation path was missed in that migration.

## Why This Fix
1. Replace the bare `reader.read()` with `readChunkWithIdleTimeout(reader, bodyIdleTimeoutMs, onIdleTimeout)`
2. Add `readChunkWithIdleTimeout` to the `src/plugin-sdk/media-runtime.ts` barrel export so extension code can import it

This is:
- **Consistent**: Uses the same utility as Signal REST, media-core, and other body-reading paths
- **Minimal**: 3 files changed, 48 lines
- **Safe**: `readChunkWithIdleTimeout` clears the timer on success and only fires when `reader.read()` genuinely stalls

## User Impact
- **Before**: A stalled SSE response body after headers arrive leaves image generation hanging indefinitely
- **After**: The stalled body read fails with `"OpenAI Codex image generation response body stalled after 30000ms"`, allowing the caller to report failure

## Evidence
- **Before**: Bare `reader.read()` on a stalled `ReadableStream` hangs until the process is killed (exit 124 from `timeout 10s` guard)
- **After**: Regression test verifies `readChunkWithIdleTimeout` rejects stalled reads with "stalled" error

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on upstream/main — bare reader.read())
```bash
$ PROOF_MODE=before timeout 10s node --import tsx scripts/proof-openai-image-body-timeout.mjs
=== BEFORE (bodyIdleTimeout=none) ===
FAIL: body read hanging after 8000ms — no idle timeout protection
EXIT: 1
```
The process was killed by the 8-second guard. Without idle timeout, `reader.read()` waits forever on a stalled body stream.

### After (with fix — regression test)
```bash
$ npx vitest run extensions/openai/image-generation-provider.test.ts \
    -t "rejects Codex image SSE response bodies that stall after sending headers"

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed | 69 skipped (70)
```
The regression test creates a `ReadableStream` that sends one valid SSE event then stalls, and asserts the provider rejects with `"stalled"`.

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `git diff --check` clean
- New regression test: `"rejects Codex image SSE response bodies that stall after sending headers"` — creates a `ReadableStream` that sends one valid SSE event then stalls, asserts the provider rejects with `"stalled"`
- Added missing barrel export: `readChunkWithIdleTimeout` from `src/plugin-sdk/media-runtime.ts`

target.title: feat(memory): add multi-slot memory role architecture
target.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes a memory-plugin architecture flaw: OpenClaw currently has one exclusive `plugins.slots.memory` owner even though the product, docs, bundled plugins, and runtime behavior already treat “memory” as several different responsibilities.

Today, factual recall, auto-capture, compaction, dreaming/consolidation, and user/session modeling are all forced through the same global selector. That makes documented memory stacks impossible or brittle: selecting one memory provider can unintentionally displace another provider that owns a different responsibility.

This PR corrects that mismatch by introducing purpose-specific memory role slots:

- `memory.recall`
- `memory.capture`
- `memory.compaction`
- `memory.dreaming`
- `memory.userModel`

The new role slots are the mechanism. The fix is that OpenClaw can now represent the memory architecture it already documents and partially implements.

## What Problem This Solves

This is a flaw fix, not just a feature request.

OpenClaw’s memory ecosystem is already multi-role:

- `memory-core` / QMD provide local factual recall/search over project memory, session transcripts, and Markdown/QMD corpora.
- Honcho provides cross-session user, agent, and session modeling.
- LanceDB provides embedding-backed long-term recall and auto-capture.
- Active Memory orchestrates recall before generation by using whichever provider owns recall.
- Memory Wiki compiles durable memory into a companion knowledge vault rather than replacing active memory.
- Dreaming/consolidation is a separate runtime responsibility from ordinary recall.

The current `plugins.slots.memory` contract cannot express that architecture. It treats every `kind: "memory"` provider as competing for one owner slot, even when the providers are designed to do different jobs. That leads to three concrete problems:

1. **Documented combinations are not representable.** Configs such as builtin/QMD recall + Honcho user modeling, LanceDB capture + local recall, or Active Memory over a selected recall provider cannot be modeled cleanly through one memory owner.
2. **Runtime behavior depends on exceptions and side paths.** Plugins that should compose have to rely on context-engine ownership, sidecar behavior, fallback logic, or plugin-specific handling instead of a shared contract.
3. **Diagnostics and lifecycle handling become misleading.** Startup, validation, status, doctor repair, skill publishing, uninstall cleanup, runtime memory resolution, and SDK-facing aliases need to know which provider owns which memory responsibility.

So while this PR adds new public config keys, the intent is corrective: make the config/runtime contract match the memory system OpenClaw already exposes.

## User Impact / Intended Outcome

After this PR, OpenClaw can express memory stacks that were previously documented or implied but not cleanly configurable:

- `memory-core` or QMD can own factual recall while Honcho owns user/session modeling.
- LanceDB can own recall and/or capture without forcing unrelated memory roles through the same selector.
- Active Memory can use the configured `memory.recall` provider instead of depending on hard-coded assumptions.
- Dreaming/consolidation can be selected separately from ordinary recall where supported.
- Memory Wiki can remain a companion compiled-knowledge layer beside active memory providers.
- Existing configs using `plugins.slots.memory` continue to work as recall selection.
- `openclaw doctor --fix` can migrate/canonicalize non-conflicting legacy memory-slot config while preserving the legacy key for plugin compatibility.

## Linked Context

Closes #60572.

Directly related memory-composition requests and prior proposals:

- #38874: supplementary/additive memory plugins alongside the primary memory slot.
- #2306: earlier closed PR proposing stackable memory plugins.
- #2080: earlier request for multiple simultaneous memory plugins and emerging memory architectures.
- #77714: pluggable persistent memory backend demand.

Dreaming and memory-role separation context:

- #85473: future protocol work for making dreaming implementable by non-`memory-core` memory plugins. This PR adds the `memory.dreaming` slot contract but does not implement that full protocol.
- #63067 and #65411: prior work around keeping dreaming behavior available when another plugin owns the legacy memory slot.
- #62275: previous selected-slot dreaming config behavior.

Runtime/diagnostic slot handling context:

- #76567 and #76495: configured memory-slot runtime checks should load/consult the selected memory plugin.
- #78540: doctor/status memory diagnostics could misreport configured memory providers.
- #76550: stale `plugins.slots.*` references could leave config unrecoverable until doctor cleanup was broadened.

Context-engine compatibility context:

- #77063, #77185, #76576, and #81843: context-engine registration and LosslessClaw-adjacent failures shaped the compatibility review for preserving the existing global `plugins.slots.contextEngine` behavior while rejecting unsupported per-agent `contextEngine` config.

Future API/RFC context:

- #70823: future machine-readable slot ownership/provenance. This PR intentionally keeps scalar plugin IDs and solves the memory role composition layer first.

Memory-plugin interop research: the [supporting research document](https://github.com/kklouzal/rfcs/blob/rfc/multi-slot-memory-role-architecture/rfcs/0009/memory-plugin-interop-research.md) validates this PR as necessary architecture work, not optional extensibility: OpenClaw's own documentation already describes memory as a composable ecosystem where builtin/QMD recall, Honcho user/session modeling, LanceDB recall/capture, Active Memory orchestration, dreaming/consolidation, and Memory Wiki compilation can coexist, but current `origin/main` collapses every `kind: "memory"` provider into one exclusive `plugins.slots.memory` owner, making those documented combinations impossible or dependent on brittle exceptions. PR #88504 closes that product/docs/runtime gap by replacing the single memory owner with explicit role slots — `memory.recall`, `memory.capture`, `memory.compaction`, `memory.dreaming`, and `memory.userModel` — while preserving legacy `memory` as a recall shorthand, so the documented memory-plugin interop story becomes actually representable in config and runtime behavior.

## What Changes

- Adds canonical memory role slots: `memory.recall`, `memory.capture`, `memory.compaction`, `memory.dreaming`, and `memory.userModel`.
- Keeps legacy `plugins.slots.memory` as a backward-compatible shorthand for `memory.recall` during an extended migration window.
- Adds per-agent memory role-slot overrides under `agents.list[*].plugins.slots`, limited to memory roles plus legacy `memory`.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where QA Lab users running the parent process under Bun could wait indefinitely before child gateway or CLI startup when the operating-system Node lookup stalls.

target.title: fix: Control UI avatar initial breaks on emoji display names
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent's display name begins with an emoji or other astral Unicode character, the Control UI rendered a broken/garbled avatar initial (a lone UTF-16 surrogate half / replacement character) instead of the intended glyph. This PR fixes that by using `Intl.Segmenter` to extract complete grapheme clusters.

## Summary

- **Problem**: Avatar initial used `.slice(0, 1)` (first UTF-16 code unit), breaking on emoji/astral Unicode.
- **Solution**: New `deriveAvatarInitial` helper using `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: "grapheme"`. Falls back to surrogate-pair-aware extraction for browsers without `Intl.Segmenter` (Firefox 114-124).
- **What changed**:
  - `ui/src/lib/avatar.ts` — `deriveAvatarInitial` with feature detection + fallback (no behavior change for ASCII)
  - `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.ts` — sidebar chip avatar uses helper
  - `ui/src/components/agent-select.ts` — agent selector fallback uses helper
  - `ui/src/components/app-sidebar-agent-menu.ts` — agent menu row initial uses helper
  - `ui/src/pages/agents/panels-overview.ts` — agents overview identity editor avatar uses helper
  - `ui/src/e2e/avatar-initial-emoji.e2e.test.ts` — dedicated real-Chromium E2E covering all four surfaces
- **All four call sites now share the identical `(deriveAvatarInitial(...) || "?")` empty-input fallback** for consistent behavior.
- **What did NOT change**: ASCII names; other `.slice()` sites (ASCII-only inputs); the plugin monogram in `ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.ts` (see coordination note).

## Rebased onto current `main`

Rebased onto current `main` (`55a822dc687`). The upstream `app-sidebar.ts` refactor (now extending `AppSidebarMenusElement`, ~688 LOC) moved the chip-avatar fallback; the affected call site still exists and was reapplied at `app-sidebar.ts:615-617`. Import-block conflict from the refactor was resolved manually. The rebased diff against `main` is exactly the 8 files above (+319 / -7).

## The four affected surfaces

A full scan of remaining `.slice(0, 1)` avatar-initial fallback sites found all four **live** surfaces sharing the identical bug:

- `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.ts` — sidebar chip avatar
- `ui/src/components/agent-select.ts` — agent selector dropdown fallback
- `ui/src/components/app-sidebar-agent-menu.ts` — agent menu row initial
- `ui/src/pages/agents/panels-overview.ts` — agents overview identity editor avatar

All now route through `deriveAvatarInitial` and are covered by the E2E below.

## Browser Compatibility

- **With `Intl.Segmenter`** (Firefox 125+, Chrome 87+, Safari 14.1+): complete grapheme clusters preserved (emoji, joined emoji, flags, skin-tone).
- **Without `Intl.Segmenter`** (Firefox 114-124): first complete code point extracted (surrogate-pair-aware), no garbled surrogate half.

## Evidence

**Real browser proof** (Playwright real Chromium, mocked Gateway), all four avatar surfaces, captured on the rebased `main`:

```text
$ OPENCLAW_CAPTURE_UI_PROOF=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
    --config test/vitest/vitest.ui-e2e.config.ts \
    ui/src/e2e/avatar-initial-emoji.e2e.test.ts

✓ renders the emoji grapheme initial in the sidebar chip and agent menu row
✓ renders the emoji grapheme initial in the agent selector dropdown
✓ renders the emoji grapheme initial in the agents overview identity editor
3 passed
```

Each surface's rendered avatar text is asserted `.toBe("🚀")` — the intact grapheme cluster, not a dangling surrogate half — read from the real browser DOM. Full-page screenshots captured locally (NOT committed, per repo visual-proof policy): `.artifacts/control-ui-e2e/avatar-initial-emoji/{01-sidebar-chip-emoji,02-agent-selector-emoji,03-agents-overview-emoji}.png`.

**Unit + component tests**:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts ui/src/components/agent-select.test.ts
20 passed
```

Helper unit tests cover both the `Intl.Segmenter` path and the stubbed-`undefined` fallback path (emoji, ZWJ family, flags, skin-tone, ASCII, empty/null/undefined). Typecheck `pnpm tsgo:ui` exit 0; `oxfmt`/`oxlint` clean on touched files.

## Coordination with sibling PR #105240

Sibling PR #105240 (`fix(control-ui): preserve emoji in plugin fallback monograms`) is a separate, non-overlapping change that touches **only** `ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.ts`. It is not affected by this PR and was left untouched. No merge conflict is expected between the two.

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage: helper unit test + component test + dedicated real-browser E2E.
- Target files: `ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts`, `ui/src/components/agent-select.test.ts`, `ui/src/e2e/avatar-initial-emoji.e2e.test.ts`.
- Scenarios locked in:
  - Helper: emoji, joined emoji (ZWJ), flags, skin-tone variant, ASCII, empty/null, and the `Intl.Segmenter`-unavailable fallback path.
  - Surfaces: sidebar chip, agent menu row, agent selector dropdown, agents overview identity editor — all assert the intact `🚀` grapheme.

target.title: fix(responses): skip non-JSON thinking signatures safely
target.body:
## Summary
Wrap `JSON.parse(block.thinkingSignature)` in a try-catch so malformed JSON signatures are safely skipped instead of throwing an unhandled `SyntaxError`.

## What Problem This Solves
In `convertResponsesMessages` at `openai-responses-transport.ts:1057`, the code intends to skip non-JSON `thinkingSignature` values (per the inline comment). However, the guard only checks whether the string starts with `{` — it does not protect against strings like `{not valid json}` that start with `{` but are not valid JSON.

If such a malformed signature is encountered, `JSON.parse` throws an unhandled `SyntaxError` that propagates through the message conversion pipeline instead of being silently skipped.

**Code evidence**: In `src/agents/openai-responses-transport.ts:1054-1061`, the `startsWith("{")` check at line 1050 correctly filters out plain-text provenance tags but does not guard against strings that start with `{` yet are not valid JSON.

## Root Cause
- The check at line 1050 (`block.thinkingSignature.startsWith("{")`) correctly filters out plain-text provenance tags (e.g. `"reasoning"`, `"content"`) that don't start with `{`, but it does not handle the case where the content starts with `{` yet is not valid JSON.
- The `JSON.parse` call at line 1057 has no try-catch.
- Trigger: a replayed/imported transcript containing a thinking block whose `thinkingSignature` is `{not valid json}` or similar malformed input.

## Why This Fix
A try-catch with `continue` implements the documented intent — skip non-JSON signatures — for all cases, not just those that fail the prefix check. This is a minimal 8-line change that does not alter the behavior for valid JSON signatures.

## User Impact
- **Before**: a malformed thinking signature in a replayed/imported transcript crashes the message conversion with `SyntaxError`, potentially breaking the entire inference pipeline
- **After**: malformed signatures are silently skipped, matching the documented intent

## Evidence
- Real behavior proof shows `SyntaxError` on main vs safe skip with fix (see below)
- `pnpm check` passed on the fix branch
- No behavior change for valid JSON signatures

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node scripts/proof-responses-nonjson-signature.mjs
=== BEFORE (on main) ===
Input: block.thinkingSignature = "{not valid json}"
Valid signature      → {"type":"reasoning","text":"hello"} (OK)
FAIL: SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2)
Result: unhandled exception propagates through message conversion pipeline
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node scripts/proof-responses-nonjson-signature.mjs
=== AFTER (with fix) ===
Valid signature      → {"type":"reasoning","text":"hello"} (OK)
Malformed signature  → skipped (null)
PASS: malformed signature safely skipped, no exception thrown
```

- `pnpm check` passed
- `git diff --check` clean
- Existing related tests (`transport-message-transform.test.ts`: 28 tests) continue to pass

target.title: fix(process): UTF-8 command output corrupts at Windows byte limits
target.body:
Related: #106495

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where byte-capped UTF-8 command output on Windows could be corrupted when the cap split a multibyte character. The retained incomplete UTF-8 prefix was passed through Windows console-code-page auto-detection, so output such as `a` followed by a partial emoji could decode with an invalid trailing character instead of the longest valid UTF-8 prefix, `a`.

This affects the SSH node-pairing identity probe because OpenSSH returns the remote JSON stream as UTF-8 while the probe keeps only the first 64 KiB.

## Why This Change Was Made

The process runner now has a narrow UTF-8-specific entry point for commands whose output encoding is defined. It applies the existing byte-boundary cleanup on every platform and decodes the retained bytes as UTF-8. The default command runner keeps its existing Windows console-code-page auto-detection, including GBK and other legacy encodings.

The SSH node-pairing probe opts into the UTF-8 path. No SSH trust, pairing eligibility, timeout, command construction, public configuration, or protocol behavior changes.

## User Impact

Windows gateways no longer corrupt a byte-capped SSH identity stream when truncation lands inside a UTF-8 character. Complete legacy-code-page command output remains unchanged.

## Evidence

- RED: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/process/exec.windows.test.ts` returned a corrupted partial character with 3 truncated bytes instead of `a` with 5 truncated bytes.
- GREEN: focused process, Windows mock, Windows integration routing, encoding, and gateway tests passed: 87 tests passed and 2 platform-specific tests skipped on Linux.
- Legacy control: a truncated CP936 buffer containing the complete `a测` prefix remains `a测` with the original auto-detecting runner.
- Tooling coverage: `test/package-scripts.test.ts` and `test/scripts/openclaw-cross-os-release-workflow.test.ts` passed (20 tests).
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo` passed.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check`, `run-oxlint.mjs`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh `codex review --base upstream/main` found the initial legacy-code-page regression; the implementation was revised to isolate UTF-8 decoding, and the final review reported no defect.
- Exact-head Windows 2025 proof and `pnpm test:windows:ci` passed on `e22cfd34043e253010e2e5f83e4afb2077dda1ad`: https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29510723363/job/87663176141

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** Byte-capped UTF-8 stdout and stderr on Windows retain the longest complete UTF-8 prefix instead of passing an incomplete character to console-code-page decoding.
- **Real environment tested:** GitHub-hosted Windows 2025 (`Windows_NT 10.0.26100 x64`) on exact PR head `e22cfd34043e253010e2e5f83e4afb2077dda1ad`. The run was manually dispatched for proof and did not use a test runner or mock subprocess for the production-runner scenario.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Installed the exact-head checkout, then used `node --import tsx` to import the production `src/process/exec.ts` facade. The production runners spawned the real Windows Node executable for a three-byte head cap, separately exercised stdout and stderr, and ran a normal identity-JSON control. The same run then executed `pnpm test:windows:ci`.
- **Evidence after fix:**

    head=e22cfd34043e253010e2e5f83e4afb2077dda1ad
    platform=win32
    os=Windows_NT 10.0.26100 x64
    default_head.code_points=U+0061,U+FFFD
    default_head.truncated_bytes=3
    utf8_head.code_points=U+0061
    utf8_head.replacement_character=false
    utf8_head.truncated_bytes=5
    utf8_stderr.code=7
    utf8_stderr.code_points=U+0061
    utf8_stderr.replacement_character=false
    utf8_stderr.truncated_bytes=5
    identity_json_control.code=0
    identity_json_control.unchanged=true

- **Observed result after fix:** The unchanged default path reproduced the invalid partial-character decode. The UTF-8-specific production path returned `a` for both stdout and stderr, contained no replacement character, and accounted for all five omitted bytes. A normal identity JSON payload was returned unchanged with exit code 0.
- **What was not tested:** A physical Windows gateway connected to a separate SSH server or a live device-pairing approval. The changed real Windows child-process capture, UTF-8 boundary cleanup, stdout/stderr decoding, normal JSON control, and Windows CI test path were exercised directly.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low and localized. Existing callers keep the same automatic Windows decoding behavior. Only callers using the new internal UTF-8 runner receive forced UTF-8 decoding and boundary cleanup; this PR changes the SSH identity probe only.

target.title: fix(plugins): clone registration record metadata for transactional rollback isolation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #106647 — two related rollback isolation bugs in plugin transaction snapshots:

1. **Registry record sharing**: Shallow spread (`[...value]`, `{ ...value }`, `new Map(value)`) only copied container references. Registration record objects inside arrays, Maps, and objects were shared between live registry and snapshot, so metadata mutations during a failed plugin's `register()` leaked through rollback.

2. **Active record scalar/flag leakage**: The loader (`loader-runtime-candidate.ts:492-531`) creates a transaction with the PluginRecord NOT yet in the registry. During `register()`, the plugin API mutates both the registry AND the record's mutable fields — id-collection arrays AND scalar counters (`httpRoutes`, `hookCount`) AND flags (`configSchema`, `enabled`). The original `activeRecord` snapshot only captured arrays, leaving scalars and flags to leak through to `recordPluginError`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two changes work together:

**`cloneRegistryEntry`** — replaces flat container copies in `snapshotPluginRegistry`. Shallow-clones individual registration records while preserving opaque plugin-owned class instances (providers, services, channels, harnesses, resolvers) by reference. Detail: for plain objects, copies each own-property — Dates become `new Date(val)`, arrays become `[...val]`, other values stay by reference.

**`snapshotActiveRecord`** — now reuses `cloneRegistryEntry` on the full PluginRecord instead of only capturing arrays. This restores every transaction-owned mutable field on rollback: arrays, scalars (`httpRoutes`, `hookCount`), booleans (`configSchema`, `enabled`, `memorySlotSelected`), and Dates (`failedAt`). Runtime objects (`configUiHints`, `configJsonSchema`, `contracts`) are preserved by reference identity.

Both captures cover all three registry container shapes: arrays, Maps, and plain objects.

All three production callers (`loader-runtime-candidate.ts`, `loader-channel-runtime.ts`, `loader-cli-registry.ts`) pass `activeRecord`.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. Internal correctness fix ensuring rollback isolation works as documented.

## Evidence

### Regression proof: before vs after (arrays + scalars + runtime identity)

Run `node_modules/.bin/tsx _proof-regression.ts`:

```
── main (before): shallow container copies, no activeRecord ──
  registry cleared:       yes
  record.toolNames:       LEAKED
  record.httpRoutes:      LEAKED
  record.hookCount:       LEAKED
  record.configSchema:    LEAKED
  Verdict: BUG — scalars and arrays leaked through rollback

── PR (after): cloneRegistryEntry registry + full activeRecord ──
  registry cleared:       yes
  record.toolNames:       restored
  record.httpRoutes:      restored
  record.hookCount:       restored
  record.configSchema:    restored
  runtime obj identity:   preserved (===)
  Verdict: FIXED — all metadata restored, references preserved
```

### Test suite: 9/9 pass

```sh
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/plugin-registration-transaction.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
```

New test (`"restores the active PluginRecord's arrays and scalars after a failed registration"`) mutates arrays (`toolNames`, `hookNames`, `providerIds`) AND scalars (`httpRoutes: 5`, `hookCount: 3`, `configSchema: true`, `memorySlotSelected: true`, `enabled: false`) during simulated `register()`, then verifies ALL are restored after rollback.

New test (`"preserves runtime object identity on the active PluginRecord through rollback"`) verifies `configUiHints` object reference survives rollback intact (`===`).

### Static checks: clean

- **oxlint**: zero warnings on all changed files
- **oxfmt**: clean formatting on all changed files

target.title: fix(codex): suppress stdout/stderr stream errors in sandbox subprocesses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stdout/stderr pipe errors from Codex sandbox exec-server subprocesses (both the process RPC path and the streaming HTTP helper) could surface as unhandled Node stream `error` events, crashing the exec-server WebSocket bridge.

## Why This Change Was Made

When a Codex sandbox child process exits or its pipes break, the Node stream layer emits `error` on the child's stdout/stderr `Readable` streams. With no `error` listener attached, Node re-throws the event, which bubbles into a process-fatal unhandled error and terminates the exec-server bridge. Both subprocess owners — `processes.ts` (process RPC) and `http.ts` (streaming HTTP) — had this gap.

The fix attaches a no-op `error` listener on `child.stdout`/`child.stderr` at each spawn point, mirroring the repo-standard pattern already used in `src/agents/sessions/exec.ts`. The process `close` handler stays authoritative for lifecycle and finalization.

Rebased onto current `main`; resolved a conflict with #103617 (defer sandbox cleanup until process close), which restructured both spawn sites into a `try/catch`. The no-op listeners are now attached after the guarded spawn, preserving that ownership.

## User Impact

The Codex sandbox exec-server no longer crashes when a subprocess output pipe breaks in either the process RPC or streaming HTTP path. Output collection and close signalling continue to work normally.

## Evidence

**Production change (both subprocess owners):** after the guarded `spawn`, before the `data` listeners, each spawn site attaches no-op `error` listeners on `child.stdout`/`child.stderr` (`processes.ts`, `http.ts`), mirroring `src/agents/sessions/exec.ts`. The `close` handler stays authoritative for lifecycle/finalization.

**Real integration proof — executes the patched code outside Vitest over a real WebSocket bridge.** A standalone `tsx` harness imports and calls the real exported entry points — `startProcess()` → `runProcess()` (process-RPC owner) and `httpRequest({streamResponse:true})` → `runStreamingSandboxHttpRequest()` (HTTP owner) — over a real `ws` bridge. Only the sandbox backend seam is stubbed; the `spawn`, stdout/stderr listeners, close lifecycle, JSON-RPC notifications, and ws bridge are all real. No `spawn` module mock, no Vitest.

Process-RPC owner — real `runProcess`, real streaming child, induced real stdout/stderr pipe error; the bridge survives and stays usable:

```text

[host] inducing a real stdout/stderr pipe error on the real child ...
[host] bridge still usable after error: readProcess ok (chunks=10, exited=true)
[host] ws bridge socket.readyState = 1 (1=OPEN)
[host] child close after the error emitted process/closed = true
[host] PASS: real patched runProcess survived the induced pipe error; bridge stayed OPEN
```

Negative control on the same real path — removing the fix's real stdout error listener from the live child reproduces the pre-fix crash, proving the listener is load-bearing:

```text
[host] stripped the fix's real stdout error listener (pre-fix state)
[host] inducing a real stdout/stderr pipe error on the real child ...
[host] UNCAUGHT EPIPE: induced sandbox stdout pipe failure -> exec-server bridge host crashed
[shell] exit=1
```

HTTP owner — real `runStreamingSandboxHttpRequest` executes end-to-end with the same guards attached:

```text
[host] real httpRequest(streaming) executed end-to-end: status=200, bodyDeltas=1
[host] ws bridge socket.readyState = 1 (1=OPEN)
[host] PASS: real patched runStreamingSandboxHttpRequest executed over the real bridge with the stdout/stderr guards attached
```

<details>
<summary>Proof integration harness (executes the real exec-server entry points; backend seam stubbed, spawn/streams/bridge real)</summary>

```ts
import { WebSocket, WebSocketServer } from "ws";
import { startProcess, readProcess, terminateProcess } from "./sandbox-exec-server/processes.js";
import { httpRequest } from "./sandbox-exec-server/http.js";

let hostCrashed = false;
process.on("uncaughtException", (e) => {
  hostCrashed = true;
  console.log(`[host] UNCAUGHT ${e.message} -> exec-server bridge host crashed`);
  process.exit(1);
});

async function socketPair() {
  const wss = new WebSocketServer({ host: "127.0.0.1", port: 0 });
  await new Promise((r) => wss.once("listening", r));
  const client = new WebSocket(`ws://127.0.0.1:${wss.address().port}`);
  const server = await new Promise((res) => wss.once("connection", res));
  await new Promise((r) => client.once("open", r));
  return { wss, client, server };
}

// Stub ONLY the backend seam; buildExecSpec spawns a REAL child.
const makeExecServer = (argv) => ({
  sandbox: {
    containerWorkdir: "/tmp",
    backend: {
      buildExecSpec: async () => ({ argv, env: process.env, finalizeToken: "tok" }),
      finalizeExec: async () => {},
    },
  },
});

// mode "process-survive": run real startProcess, induce a real stdout/stderr error, assert bridge OPEN.
// mode "process-strip":   same, but managed.child.stdout.removeAllListeners("error") first -> host crashes.
// mode "http-execute":    run real httpRequest({streamResponse:true}) end-to-end over the real ws bridge.
// (full runnable harness kept in the contributor outputs)
```

</details>

**Mutation-sensitive regression test** (`sandbox-exec-server.pipe-survival.test.ts`): captures the real spawned child and emits `error` on the real `child.stdout`/`child.stderr` for both the process RPC and streaming HTTP paths, asserting each stream carries an `error` listener, that emitting the error does not throw, that the WebSocket bridge stays `OPEN`, and (process path) that the bridge still runs follow-up work. Removing either production listener makes the test fail.

```text
$ cd /tmp/openclaw-proof-101777 && cat stream-error-lifecycle.txt
```

target.title: feat: add disableBoundaryAwareCache compat option for prefix-matching prompt cache providers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where DeepSeek OpenAI-compatible users lose provider prompt-cache hits after the 6.x boundary-aware cache split placed per-turn dynamic context ahead of the stable system prompt, so the large stable instruction block stopped caching and billed input tokens climbed.

Closes #94518

Related: #91018, #90583

## Why This Change Was Made

DeepSeek uses implicit prefix-matching cache, so its leading `system` message must stay byte-stable across turns for the stable instruction block to keep hitting cache. This PR adds `compat.disableBoundaryAwareCache`, auto-enables it for DeepSeek, keeps only the stable prefix in the `system` message, and emits the below-boundary runtime suffix as a trailing `system`-role carrier after the conversation history. That keeps the latest user message byte-identical (so it stays a reusable prefix once it becomes history) and keeps runtime/approval/identity guidance at system/developer authority instead of demoting it into user content.

Non-goal / honest limit: when the below-boundary context genuinely changes every turn, accumulated conversation history still cannot be cached — DeepSeek persists a cache prefix unit at the end of each request, so a trailing carrier that changes each turn ends every request on different bytes. No message re-ordering can cache history under that condition; this PR restores the stable-prefix cache, not moving full-history reuse.

Xiaomi is kept opt-in — users can set `compat.disableBoundaryAwareCache: true` manually, but the automatic default is DeepSeek-only until Xiaomi-specific upstream cache-contract and live-behavior evidence exists. Operators can opt back into boundary-aware behavior with `compat: { disableBoundaryAwareCache: false }`.

## User Impact

DeepSeek users keep the large stable system prompt cacheable from the first turn instead of losing it whenever below-boundary runtime context updates, which lowers billed input tokens on the cost regression #94518 reports. target.title: fix(agents): remove empty parent directory on agent delete
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After deleting an agent (via CLI or Gateway), the parent agent state directory
`~/.openclaw/agents/<agentId>/` is left as an empty folder on disk. Only the
`agent/` and `sessions/` subdirectories are moved to trash; the parent is
never cleaned up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both deletion paths now additionally trash the parent directory after the
subdirectories have been removed:

- **Gateway path** (`agents.delete` handler): calls `moveToTrashBestEffort`
  on `path.dirname(agentDir)` after the existing `Promise.all` for
  subdirectory cleanup.

- **CLI fallback path** (`agentsDeleteCommand`): calls `moveToTrash` on
  `path.dirname(agentDir)` after trashing `agentDir` and `sessionsDir`.

The cleanup is best-effort — if the parent directory is not empty (e.g. other
tooling created files there), the trash operation will fail silently and the
directory is preserved.

## User Impact

No more stale empty directories accumulating under `~/.openclaw/agents/`
after repeated agent create/delete cycles.

## Evidence

### Tests (fail on main, pass on this branch)

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/agents.delete.test.ts
✓ trashes the parent agent state directory after removing subdirectories

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/agents-mutate.test.ts
✓ agents.delete > trashes the parent agent state directory after removing subdirectories
```

### Manual verification

```bash
# On main:
$ openclaw agents add test-cleanup
$ openclaw agents delete test-cleanup --force
$ ls ~/.openclaw/agents/test-cleanup/  # directory exists but is empty

# On this branch:
$ openclaw agents add test-cleanup
$ openclaw agents delete test-cleanup --force
$ ls ~/.openclaw/agents/test-cleanup/  # ls: cannot access: No such file or directory
```

target.title: fix(tts): bound OpenAI TTS contract synthesize fetch requests
target.body:
## Summary
Add a 30-second `AbortSignal.timeout()` to the OpenAI TTS speech provider's `synthesize` and `synthesizeTelephony` fetch calls in the TTS contract suites, so stalled TTS API endpoints don't hang contract tests.

## What Problem This Solves
The `buildTestOpenAISpeechProvider()` function in `src/plugins/contracts/tts-contract-suites.ts` creates a test speech provider whose `synthesize` and `synthesizeTelephony` implementations call the OpenAI TTS API via `fetch()` without any timeout signal. If the TTS endpoint accepts a TCP connection but stalls before responding, the contract test hangs indefinitely.

**Code evidence**: In `src/plugins/contracts/tts-contract-suites.ts`, both the `synthesize` (line 272) and `synthesizeTelephony` (line 295) `fetch()` calls lack a `signal` property.

## Root Cause
- The test provider implementations were authored without abort signals on their fetch calls.
- No `AbortController` or `AbortSignal.timeout()` was included.
- Trigger: a TTS API endpoint that stalls mid-connection causes the contract test suite to hang.

## Why This Fix
`AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)` is the standard pattern for bounding fetch calls throughout the codebase. The 30-second value is consistent with other HTTP timeouts in the repository (e.g., `CROSS_OS_DISCORD_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`). This is a minimal, non-invasive change — one line per fetch call.

## User Impact
- **Before**: TTS contract tests hang indefinitely when the OpenAI TTS API stalls
- **After**: TTS contract tests fail with a clear `AbortError: The operation was aborted due to timeout` after 30 seconds

## Evidence
- Real behavior proof shows no `AbortSignal` on main vs valid timeout signal with fix (see below)
- `AbortSignal.timeout()` is a standard web API — the mechanism is proven across the codebase

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node scripts/proof-tts-fetch-timeout.mjs
=== BEFORE (on main) ===
FAIL: fetch() called without AbortSignal — stalled TTS endpoint hangs indefinitely
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node scripts/proof-tts-fetch-timeout.mjs
=== AFTER (with fix) ===
PASS: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) passed to fetch() — will abort stalled request after 30s

--- AbortSignal.timeout fires after delay (proof of mechanism) ---
PASS: AbortSignal aborted after 506ms (expected ~500ms)
Reason: The operation was aborted due to timeout

This is the same AbortSignal.timeout mechanism added to the TTS fetch calls.
Before → no signal → hang. After → signal → clear abort after 30s.
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `git diff --check` clean
- Added regression test: `"passes a timeout signal to fetch in the OpenAI synthesize provider"` — mocks fetch, captures the signal, asserts it is defined and not aborted

target.title: fix(subagents): credit requester-consumed descendant completions
target.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes a lifecycle/delivery accounting gap for background and cron-owned subagent trees: when a requester actually consumes completed descendant subagent output, the descendant run is now durably credited as delivered instead of later being finalized as failed/suspended solely because no separate visible delivery event occurred.

## What Problem This Solves

Requester-owned subagent trees can legitimately consume descendant output without sending a separate descendant-visible delivery event. This is common for cron/background flows where a parent/requester gathers frozen child output, composes its own result, and then delivers that requester result outward. Before this PR, the descendant completion could remain delivery-unproven even though its output had already been consumed by the requester. Later cleanup/finalization could then classify that descendant as failed or suspended, producing delivery state that did not match real behavior. This PR gives the registry an explicit durable signal for that case: requester consumption is delivery evidence only for the exact descendant runs that were consumed, under the matching requester session/run-start window, when the requester path adopts descendant fallback output, so the consumed descendant rows do not later announce or finalize as pending just because the final outward send fails.

## User Impact / Intended Outcome

When OpenClaw can prove that a requester consumed descendant subagent output, the matching descendant run receives durable delivery credit:
- `delivery.status` is set to `"delivered"` for the matched descendant completion;
- requester-consumption metadata is persisted with the run/delivery state;
- cleanup/finalize treats `delivery.status === "delivered"` as completed delivery proof;
- normal visible-delivery paths remain required for completions that were not consumed by a requester.
The matching is intentionally narrow. Credit is only applied when all of these are true:
- the consumed run IDs are explicit;
- the requester session key matches;
- the requester run-start window matches the consuming requester run;
- the consumption kind is known;
- cron fallback credit happens when cron adopts explicit descendant fallback output for the requester result;
- nested subagent announcement credit only covers direct child run IDs that were actually included in the requester-consumed output.

This PR keeps the delivery model explicit:
- if a descendant result was visibly delivered, it is delivered;
- if a requester consumed the descendant output because cron adopted it as the requester result, the descendant is delivered by requester consumption;
- if neither happened, failure/suspension handling still applies.

## Linked Context

- Related issue: #92433 — subagent completion can be silently dropped when an announce handoff reaches a requester transcript but the requester run ends before consuming it. This PR addresses the adjacent durable-accounting problem for completions that *are* consumed by a requester.
- Related issue: #67777 — subagent completion delivery can be lost on direct-announce timeout, drain, or orphan prune. This PR does not implement the full durable inbox/spool requested there, but it narrows one delivery-accounting gap by recording proven requester consumption.
- Related issue: #86537 — suspended final delivery can expire and discard a pending subagent completion. This PR keeps requester-consumed completions from remaining indistinguishable from undelivered completions in finalization state.
- Related issue: #90299 — subagent lifecycle state can report lost active execution context while still surfacing child output. This PR contributes to lifecycle/state consistency when descendant output is actually consumed.
- Related PR: #92934 — required assistant acknowledgement for completion wake handoffs, so transcript commit alone is not treated as requester consumption. This PR complements that by adding durable credit for explicit consumed descendant run IDs.
- Related PR: #35080 — deterministic subagent announce delivery with descendant gating. This PR builds on that direction by making consumed descendant accounting durable.
- Related PR: #44205 — stale descendant cron fallback summaries. This PR keeps the same stale-vs-current discipline for requester-consumed descendant credit.
- Related PR: #95604 — Discord subagent progress feedback. This PR is not a Discord UI change, but accurate delivered/failed lifecycle state is useful to progress/failure-marker consumers.
No exact existing issue/PR was found for `markDescendantCompletionConsumedByRequester` or this exact requester-consumed credit mechanism, so this PR should stand as the focused implementation thread for that behavior.

## What Changes

When OpenClaw can prove that a requester consumed descendant subagent output, the matching descendant run receives durable delivery credit:
- `delivery.status` is set to `"delivered"` for the matched descendant completion;
- requester-consumption metadata is persisted with the run/delivery state;
- cleanup/finalize treats `delivery.status === "delivered"` as completed delivery proof;
- normal visible-delivery paths remain required for completions that were not consumed by a requester.
The matching is intentionally narrow. Credit is only applied when all of these are true:
- the consumed run IDs are explicit;
- the requester session key matches;
- the requester run-start window matches the consuming requester run;
- the consumption kind is known;
- cron fallback credit happens when cron adopts explicit descendant fallback output for the requester result;
- nested subagent announcement credit only covers direct child run IDs that were actually included in the requester-consumed output.

## Implementation Notes

Core registry/runtime changes:
- Adds requester-consumed delivery metadata to subagent registry/delivery state.
- Adds a registry operation for marking descendant completions consumed by requester.
- Persists/restores the new delivery fields.
- Exposes the new runtime operation through the existing registry runtime shims.
Main files:
- `src/agents/subagent-registry-consumption.ts`
  - Implements durable requester-consumption credit.
  - Matches by requester session, explicit run IDs, and run-start window.
  - Records requester-consumption metadata and persists the updated run state.
- `src/agents/subagent-registry.types.ts`
  - Adds delivery/requester-consumption state fields.
- `src/agents/subagent-delivery-state.ts`
  - Persists and restores the new delivery fields.
- `src/agents/subagent-registry.ts`
- `src/agents/subagent-registry-runtime.ts`
- `src/agents/subagent-announce.registry.runtime.ts`
- `src/cron/isolated-agent/delivery-subagent-registry.runtime.ts`
  - Wires the new registry operation through runtime boundaries.
Requester-consumption paths:
- `src/cron/isolated-agent/subagent-followup.ts`
  - Reads completed descendant fallback replies and returns both formatted fallback text and the consumed descendant run IDs.
- `src/cron/isolated-agent/delivery-dispatch.ts`
  - Applies cron fallback consumption credit when cron adopts explicit descendant fallback output, before the final outbound send.
- `src/agents/subagent-announce.ts`
  - Credits nested/direct child completions when their output is included in the requester-consumed announcement/wake result.
  - Uses the same latest-child dedupe input for rendering and consumed-run credit so stale child rows are not credited.
- `src/agents/subagent-announce-output.ts`
  - Keeps latest-child dedupe reusable while preserving caller-specific fields such as `runId`.

## Tests / Verification

Coverage added or extended for:
- positive requester-consumed descendant credit;
- no credit for mismatched requester session;
- no credit outside the requester run-start window;
- no credit without explicit consumed run IDs;
- persisted/restored requester-consumption delivery fields;
- cron fallback credit only after successful outbound delivery;
- cleanup/finalize treating `delivery.status === "delivered"` as proof;
- nested/direct child announcement credit;
- stale-vs-current child dedupe, including a negative assertion that stale child run IDs are not credited when stale output is not rendered.
Primary test files:
- `src/agents/subagent-registry-consumption.test.ts`
- `src/agents/subagent-delivery-state.test.ts`
- `src/agents/subagent-registry-completion.test.ts`
- `src/agents/subagent-registry.lifecycle-retry-grace.e2e.test.ts`
- `src/agents/subagent-announce.format.e2e.test.ts`

## Evidence

### Rebase/Squash/Proof

target.title: fix(googlechat): media downloads can grow unbounded without a size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where direct callers of the Google Chat media download API could omit `maxBytes` and let a successful media response buffer through an uncapped `arrayBuffer()` call. The normal inbound attachment path already passes a configured cap, but the exported helper still had an uncapped fallback.

## Why This Change Was Made

Google Chat media downloads now use the existing 20 MiB Google Chat media default whenever callers do not provide a stricter cap. Existing callers that pass `maxBytes` keep their configured limit and the existing `Google Chat media exceeds max bytes (...)` error contract.

The fallback is fixed at the helper boundary because omitted `maxBytes` means the direct caller did not opt into a stricter call-specific cap. Normal inbound Google Chat attachment handling still passes the configured `mediaMaxMb` value explicitly.

## User Impact

Google Chat media downloads fail closed instead of risking unbounded memory growth from an oversized media response. Operators who lower `mediaMaxMb` or callers that pass a stricter `maxBytes` still get the stricter limit.

## Evidence

- Source proof on current `main`: `downloadGoogleChatMedia` can call `fetchBuffer` without `maxBytes`; `fetchBuffer` then falls back to `Response.arrayBuffer()` on successful responses.

target.title: fix(e2e): bound non-root installer fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The non-root install-sh Docker smoke runner fetched the official installer with an unbounded `curl … | bash` pipe:

```sh
# scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh:65 (before)
curl -fsSL "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

`curl` has no total-time or connect-time limit by default. If `$INSTALL_URL` (defaults to `https://openclaw.bot/install.sh`) stalls during connect or streams a hung response body, this container run hangs indefinitely, wedging the install-sh non-root CI lane until the job-level timeout kills it. That burns a full runner slot and produces no actionable signal.

This is the same hang class already fixed for the sibling e2e runner in #108810 (`scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh` uses `mktemp` + `curl --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o … && bash …`). The non-root runner was left on the old piped form.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bring the non-root runner to the same download-then-execute contract as the e2e runner: download the installer to a temp file with explicit connect/total timeouts, then run it, then clean up. Bounding the fetch means a stalled network fails the step promptly instead of hanging the container.

`--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120` matches the values already merged across the installer/download fixes in this area (#108810, #108911, etc.).

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change to the installer itself. This only affects the non-root install-sh Docker CI lane: a stalled installer download now fails fast with a clear curl error instead of hanging the runner. Same install semantics on success.

## Evidence

Problem code (still unbounded on current `main`):

```
$ git show origin/main:scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh | sed -n '64,65p'
echo "==> Run installer (non-root user)"
curl -fsSL "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

After (this PR):

```sh
echo "==> Run installer (non-root user)"
installer="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$installer"' EXIT
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer" "$INSTALL_URL"
bash "$installer"
```

Focused test run (new test `downloads the non-root installer completely before execution` + full file):

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  78 passed (78)
```

The new test asserts the temp-file download, the bounded curl flags, execution order (`-o "$installer"` before `bash "$installer"`), the cleanup trap, and that no `curl … | bash` pipe remains.

Additional checks:

```
$ bash -n scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh   # syntax OK
$ oxfmt --check test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts   # All matched files use the correct format
$ git diff --check   # clean
```

Diff: +8/−1 prod (`run.sh`), +13 test.

### What was not tested

Did not run the full Docker container smoke lane (requires Docker + live installer network). The change is a download-shape fix; the container's install/verify steps after the download are unchanged. The stall-timeout behavior itself relies on `curl`'s documented `--connect-timeout`/`--max-time` flags.

### Scope boundary

Only `scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh` and its test. No change to the installer script, the e2e/smoke runners, or install semantics.

### Related

- #108810 — same fix for the e2e runner (this mirrors that pattern).

## Runtime proof (added)

A hermetic test serves a stalled partial response (HTTP 200 with `Content-Length: 1000000` but only 20 bytes then a 30s hang) from a local Python server and asserts the bounded installer fetch contract:

- `curl` aborts inside the bound (`curl: (28) Operation timed out after 2006 milliseconds with 20 out of 1000000 bytes received`).
- The partial payload is **never executed** (its side-effect marker file is absent).
- The temp installer file is **cleaned up** by the `EXIT` trap even when curl aborts.

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts -t stalled
✓ aborts a stalled <non-root / official-installer> fetch inside the bound without running partial payload
Tests  1 passed | 72 skipped (73)
```

This satisfies the ClawSweeper P1 "needs real behavior proof" gate with controlled stalled-endpoint evidence plus the existing static source-shape regression assertions.

target.title: Apply consented grouped Claw updates
target.body:
## Summary

- Extends experimental `claws update` from the read-only plan in #102959 to consented mutation across agent config, managed workspace files, packages, MCP declarations, cron jobs, and root provenance.
- Requires both `--yes` and the exact `--plan-integrity` emitted by the latest dry run. Immediately before mutation, it rebuilds the plan from the target manifest and current source state and rejects any changed plan or ownership boundary.
- Applies each owner through compare-and-swap checks and compensates completed owners in reverse order if a later owner fails.
- Advances root package/version/integrity provenance only after every owner succeeds.
- Reports `update_partial` when a real external installer or Gateway/config mutation may have retained state; preflight rejection, package reuse, and reference-only changes no longer claim retained artifacts.

This remains behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1` and is the mutation stage for the preceding read-only update plan.

Stack references:
- RFC: openclaw/rfcs#27
- Base/read-only planner: #102959
- Control UI plugin lifecycle alignment: #103176

## Lifecycle contract

```bash
openclaw claws update <claw-or-agent> --from <source> --dry-run --json
openclaw claws update <claw-or-agent> --from <source> \
  --yes --plan-integrity <sha256-from-dry-run> --json
```

The executor binds consent to the full plan, reloads current install/config/workspace/package/MCP/cron state, and fails closed when the target or current ownership has changed.

- **Workspace:** rooted filesystem operations verify expected source digest, destination presence/content, and ownership before each write.
- **Packages:** exact ClawHub versions use the shared installers. Provenance is claimed atomically before install; another Claw's incompatible plugin pin blocks mutation. Remove releases only this Claw's reference. Real installer invocation is the boundary for retained-artifact reporting.
- **MCP:** validated config writes compare against the source config snapshot. Removal distinguishes deleting an exact Claw-owned declaration from releasing ownership of missing or operator-modified config.
- **Cron:** Gateway-owned operations converge on stable Claw declaration keys and preserve explicit partial-state semantics for non-transactional scheduler writes.
- **Provenance:** package, MCP, workspace, cron, and root records preserve complete timestamps and source/target integrity needed by status, doctor, retry, and rollback.

## Real behavior proof

An isolated WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 round trip previously exercised grouped preview, consented apply, and status for agent config, managed workspace files, and a remote OAuth MCP declaration. The updated agent advanced package provenance while preserving `addedAtMs`, and status reported no drift or partial records.

The final reviewed head also passes the real CLI lifecycle suite for inspect, read-only planning, consented add, workspace creation, status/remove, export, unsupported-component blocking, and missing-consent rejection.

Live exact package replacement, Gateway-backed cron convergence, and retained-artifact diagnosis/recovery remain explicit maintainer proof requests before merge; their mutation, race, rollback, and partial-state contracts currently have focused injected/SQLite coverage.

## Validation

- 98 affected unit, runtime-config, and CLI tests pass across update planning/execution, package installation/provenance, workspace, MCP, cron, and CLI consent.
- 8 real lifecycle E2E tests pass.
- Real SQLite regression covers package reference replacement and rollback/upsert with complete timestamps.
- Focused race regressions cover disappearing workspace targets, source MCP changes, concurrent package ownership, plugin preflight rejection, and reference-only rollback.
- Touched-file `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` pass.
- `codex review --base upstream/user/giodl/claws-pr11-update-plan`: no concrete actionable regressions.

## Stack note

This is a draft stacked PR. Do not merge it before #102959 and the earlier Claws ownership/lifecycle slices settle.

target.title: fix(tools-manager): bound GitHub release JSON response read
target.body:
## Summary
Replace unbounded `response.json()` with `readProviderJsonResponse` in `getLatestVersion` so the GitHub API response body is read through a bounded buffer with descriptive error wrapping.

## What Problem This Solves
In `src/agents/utils/tools-manager.ts:159`, `getLatestVersion` calls `await response.json()` directly on the GitHub API response. This reads the entire response body into memory without any size limit, and throws raw `SyntaxError` on malformed JSON without any context about which API failed.

**Code evidence**: at `tools-manager.ts:159`, the code previously used `(await response.json()) as { tag_name: string }` — an unbounded read of the full response body with no error context.

## Root Cause
The function uses `fetchWithSsrFGuard` which provides connection timeout and SSR protection, but after the connection succeeds, the response body is read entirely via `.json()` with no size limit and no descriptive error wrapping. The `downloadFile` function in the same file already uses Content-Length checks for downloads, but `getLatestVersion` lacked equivalent bounds.

## Why This Fix
`readProviderJsonResponse` is the standard bounded reader used by provider HTTP callers throughout the codebase. It:
1. Caps response body reads at 16 MiB via `readResponseWithLimit`
2. Wraps malformed JSON `SyntaxError` with a descriptive label (`"GitHub release check: malformed JSON response"`) so callers can diagnose which API failed
3. Is already used by other provider HTTP paths (e.g., `readProviderJsonObjectResponse`)

## User Impact
- **Before**: malformed GitHub API responses throw raw `SyntaxError` with no diagnostic context; arbitrarily large responses are buffered into memory
- **After**: responses are bounded to 16 MiB; malformed JSON produces descriptive errors identifying the `GitHub release check` API as the source

## Evidence
- Real behavior proof shows `response.json()` reads 1 MiB unbounded and throws raw `SyntaxError` on malformed JSON, while `readProviderJsonResponse` wraps errors with a descriptive label (see below)
- `pnpm check` passed on the fix branch

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-bounded-github-release-json.mjs
=== BEFORE (on main) ===
--- Large response (1 MiB) via response.json() ---
FAIL: response.json() read 1024 KiB into memory with no size limit

--- Malformed JSON via response.json() ---
FAIL: SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2)
Result: raw SyntaxError propagates — caller has no context about which API failed
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-bounded-github-release-json.mjs
=== AFTER (with fix) ===
--- Valid response via readProviderJsonResponse ---
Result: {"tag_name":"v1.2.3"}
PASS: valid JSON parsed within bounds

--- Malformed JSON via readProviderJsonResponse ---
PASS: GitHub release check: malformed JSON response
Result: error includes the provider label so callers can diagnose which API failed
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `git diff --check` clean
- Existing `tools-manager.test.ts` tests (16) continue to pass

target.title: fix(google): reject malformed provider media base64
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Google provider responses could include malformed inline audio or video base64 that Node would decode permissively instead of rejecting.

## Why This Change Was Made

Google music, speech, video generation, and Realtime Live audio now share a strict base64 decoder before materializing provider-returned media. The Google-specific decoder accepts both standard base64 and Google ProtoJSON-valid base64url payloads before canonical validation, while inline video bytes reuse the existing generated-video byte cap before decode so oversized payloads fail before allocating the full buffer.

## User Impact

Users get a clear provider error for malformed Google media responses without rejecting valid base64url media that Google may return. Realtime Live malformed inline audio is routed through `onError` without emitting corrupt audio, and operators keep the existing video media cap behavior without permissive base64 decoding.

## Evidence

Live Google TTS run through the production `buildGoogleSpeechProvider().synthesize()` entrypoint; this was captured on the earlier PR head `f36b9f96544a6416e51712ee3881e682409df825` before the base64url compatibility follow-up, and the same entrypoint remains covered by focused regression tests on current head `4f77e023235`:

```text
$ GEMINI_API_KEY=<redacted> node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-providers.config.ts extensions/google/live-google-tts-proof.test.ts --reporter verbose

=== LIVE GOOGLE TTS PROOF ===
entrypoint=buildGoogleSpeechProvider().synthesize
started_at=2026-07-14T12:47:34.918Z
model=gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview
voice=Kore
proxy=explicit-redacted
api_key=redacted
ok=true
output_format=wav
file_extension=.wav
audio_bytes=109484
pcm_payload_bytes=109440
wav_header=RIFF/WAVE
```

The focused tests drive the real exported provider entrypoints — `buildGoogleSpeechProvider().synthesize()`, `buildGoogleMusicGenerationProvider().generateMusic()`, `buildGoogleVideoGenerationProvider().generateVideo()`, and `buildGoogleRealtimeVoiceProvider().createBridge()` — with crafted valid, malformed, and oversized provider responses; the `decodeGoogleProviderBase64` guard runs as real production code on those response paths:

- **Valid path preserved:** legitimate standard base64 and base64url audio/video still materialize; the video byte cap reuses the existing generated-video limit rather than a new arbitrary value, so valid traffic is not truncated.
- **Malformed rejected:** music, speech, video, and Google Live malformed inline base64 each raise a provider-specific error instead of decoding corrupt bytes; the Live path does not call `onAudio`.
- **Oversized rejected before buffering:** inline video bytes, direct URI downloads, and SDK file-handle downloads exceeding the media cap fail before unbounded allocation.

target.title: fix(dreaming): drop heartbeat assistant responses from dream corpus
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The dreaming ingestion pipeline filters heartbeat **user** messages (containing `[OpenClaw heartbeat poll]`) via `sanitizeSessionText`, but the paired **assistant** response was only dropped when it was the exact string `HEARTBEAT_OK`. Local models frequently respond with natural-language acknowledgments (e.g. "Heartbeat received. Main is active.") which pass through the sanitizer unchanged and enter the dream corpus as low-confidence memory snippets.

See issue #103720.

## Why This Change Was Made

The original text-based heartbeat detection was user-spoofable (anyone could type the heartbeat marker and trigger the drop). The fix uses **runtime provenance** (`provenance: { kind: "heartbeat" }`) attached at the source in `get-reply-run.ts`, which cannot be spoofed by user input.

For existing workspaces with heartbeat contamination, the `doctor` audit/repair system:
- Scans session-corpus files for heartbeat-derived lines via source refs
- Archives the entire session-corpus directory and clears all SQLite ingestion checkpoints so the corpus rebuilds under the new provenance filter
- Handles both file-backed sessions (`.jsonl` paths) and SQLite-backed sessions (canonical `.jsonl` paths from `sessionPathForSessionIdentity()`) via a fallback to `loadTranscriptEventsSync`
- Diary is preserved — no user-visible diary entries are lost
- Re-running repair is idempotent (no-op on clean state)

## User Impact

- **No visible change** for users without heartbeat contamination
- **Lower memory noise** for users with heartbeat-enabled sessions — average 0.58-confidence heartbeat-derived entries are removed from dream corpus
- **One-time cleanup** via `openclaw doctor` for existing workspaces
- **No data loss** — contaminated artifacts are archived before removal, normal corpus entries are preserved

target.title: fix(security): scan SKILL.md text in skill code-safety audit
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw security audit --deep` never scanned a skill's SKILL.md. A malicious workspace SKILL.md containing pipe-to-shell install patterns (`curl … | bash`), `rm -rf ~/`, secret-exfiltration, or prompt-injection produced **zero** audit findings — while the identical patterns placed in a sibling `tool.js` were immediately flagged `skills.code_safety critical`. Since SKILL.md is the primary (often only) file a skill ships, and manually-authored workspace skills are never scanned at install time, malicious skill text was invisible to the audit.

## Why This Change Was Made

The scanner already has rules written for skill *text* (`shell-pipe-to-shell` = "Skill text includes pipe-to-shell install pattern", `secret-exfiltration`, `prompt-injection-*`), and the Workshop proposal path scans PROPOSAL.md markdown. But the installed/workspace-skill audit (`collectInstalledSkillsCodeSafetyFindings`) only fed `SCANNABLE_EXTENSIONS` (JS/TS) to the scanner, skipping the markdown.

Fix: each audited skill's SKILL.md content is now scanned through `scanSkillContent` + `scanSource` (the same scanners the Workshop uses), merged into the code-safety summary. Scoped to the skills audit path — the global directory scanner's extension set is unchanged, so READMEs/docs elsewhere are not newly scanned (no false-positive flood).

## User Impact

`security audit --deep` now flags dangerous instructions in skill SKILL.md files (pipe-to-shell, prompt-injection, exfiltration), closing a security blind spot for manually-authored/workspace skills. No change to non-skill scanning.

## Evidence

- Regression test `audit-extra.async.test.ts` "scans SKILL.md text for dangerous skill instructions": **red before** ("expected skill markdown code-safety finding"), green after. 7 tests pass.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` green on Testbox; `oxfmt --check`, `git diff --check` clean.
- Autoreview: clean, no accepted/actionable findings.

target.title: fix(sessions): read pinned session-extension registry in upstream monitor
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`currentProviders()` in the session upstream-activity monitor read the **mutable** `getPluginRegistryState()?.activeRegistry` to discover session-catalog providers. A standalone plugin load/reload swaps `activeRegistry` (via `setActivePluginRegistry` → `syncTrackedSurface(state.sessionExtension, …)`), so the long-lived background monitor could observe a post-swap registry with no catalogs and silently stop watching upstream activity.

This is the same drift class fixed upstream in `session-catalog.ts`, which now reads the bootstrap-pinned `getActivePluginSessionExtensionRegistry()`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Read the pinned session-extension registry (`getActivePluginSessionExtensionRegistry()?.sessionCatalogs`) instead of the mutable `activeRegistry`. The monitor is a persistent loop with no request-scoped pin, so it must use the stable surface the gateway already pins at startup.

## User Impact

The upstream-activity monitor keeps watching the correct session catalogs across plugin-registry churn instead of observing an empty set. No config or protocol change; no migration.

## Evidence

- Regression test `session-upstream-monitor-pinned-registry.test.ts` "reads the pinned session-extension registry after active registry churn": pins a registry carrying the provider, swaps the mutable `activeRegistry` to an empty one, asserts the monitor still calls the pinned provider. **Red before the fix** (`checkUpstreamActivity` called 0 times), green after.

target.title: fix: use last valid daemon --port for status, audit, and launchd
target.body:
Related: #109292

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where daemon status, service audit, and launchd stop/restart helpers could use the wrong Gateway port when an installed service command contained repeated `--port` flags. Status/repair helpers previously returned the first valid port while Commander-style CLI parsing uses the last occurrence as the effective value.

## Why This Change Was Made

Align all three installed-service argv port readers on Commander-style **effective last** semantics:

- Shared helper `parseTcpPortFromArgs` now keeps the last valid `--port` / `--port=` value (invalid occurrences stay ignored for best-effort probes).
- Launchd lifecycle port resolution reuses that helper so stop/restart cleanup probes the same port as status/repair.
- Service audit evaluates the **last** `--port` occurrence and still reports explicit invalid state for that last value (not a silent first-match).

This matches the sibling-surface guidance on the earlier candidate fix and avoids leaving status on the last port while launchd cleanup/audit still used the first.

Compatibility: no config/API/schema change; only repeated-flag argv interpretation for daemon introspection. Performance: single linear scan, same as before. Usability: operators see consistent port selection across status, audit, and lifecycle cleanup. Security: no auth, secrets, or trust-boundary change.

## User Impact

Operators get accurate Gateway status, audit, and launchd stop/restart port selection when wrappers or stale service definitions include more than one `--port` flag.

## Evidence

Focused tests (local macOS):

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/tcp-port.test.ts src/daemon/service-audit.test.ts

[test] passed 2 Vitest shards in 32.54s
- src/infra/tcp-port.test.ts (5 tests)
- src/daemon/service-audit.test.ts (48 tests)
```

Changed-lane checks: format, conflict markers, and other static gates for the touched core files passed. Plugin SDK API baseline reports a pre-existing hash drift on current `main` with no plugin-sdk files in this diff. One `launchd.test.ts` ANSI-sanitize case is environment-sensitive under `FORCE_COLOR` and passes with `NO_COLOR=1`; it is outside this port-parser change.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: repeated `--port` flags in service argv resolve to the effective last valid port for shared status/repair parsing, and sibling audit/launchd readers no longer keep first-match semantics for the same argv shape.
- Environment: local macOS, OpenClaw checkout at branch `fix/109292-effective-daemon-port`, Node with `tsx` import of production modules.
- Current-main contrast: on main, `parseTcpPortFromArgs(['gateway','--port','18789','--port','19001'])` returned `18789` (first match). The same probe for equals-form flags also returned the first value.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```sh
node --import tsx -e "import { parseTcpPortFromArgs } from './src/infra/tcp-port.ts'; console.log(parseTcpPortFromArgs(['gateway','--port','18789','--port','19001'])); console.log(parseTcpPortFromArgs(['gateway','--port=18789','--port=19002'])); console.log(parseTcpPortFromArgs(['gateway','--port','nope','--port','19003']));"
```

target.title: fix(voice-call): unref ngrok startup timeout and mark closed on timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`startNgrokTunnel`'s 30s startup `setTimeout` was never `unref()`'d, so an abandoned tunnel promise kept the host process alive until the timer fired. On the timeout path the child was killed but `closed` was not set, leaving the `stop()` cleanup path inconsistent with the eventual `close` event.

## Why This Change Was Made

`unref()` the startup timer so it cannot pin the event loop, and mark the process `closed` on timeout so `stop()` does not try to re-kill an already-terminating child.

## User Impact

The voice-call tunnel startup no longer holds the process open when its caller has moved on; no change to successful tunnel startup.

## Evidence

- Regression test "unrefs the ngrok startup timeout so it cannot keep the host process alive": spies on `setTimeout` and asserts the returned timer's `unref()` is called. **Red before the fix** (`unref` called 0 times), green after.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.test.ts` → 16 passed.
- Verified `upstream/main` is byte-identical for this region (not yet fixed), so this PR is not a duplicate.

target.title: fix(gateway): let wizard clients control daemon installation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Remote wizard clients can already express whether onboarding should install a daemon through `OnboardOptions.installDaemon`, but the Gateway RPC contract rejected that field and `wizard.start` did not forward it.

This blocks clients that own the service lifecycle themselves, including the Windows Companion setup flow. Passing `installDaemon=false` must prevent the Gateway-hosted wizard from installing a competing daemon inside the managed environment.

Related Windows Companion work:
- openclaw/openclaw-windows-node#1000
- openclaw/openclaw-windows-node#999

## Why This Change Was Made

This keeps ownership at the existing native boundary:

- add the optional boolean to the closed `WizardStartParamsSchema`;
- forward the exact value, preserving explicit `false`, `true`, and omission;
- keep Gateway-hosted wizard runs headless with `skipUi=true`;
- suppress token-bearing terminal output with `suppressGatewayTokenOutput=true`.

No new lifecycle mechanism or client-specific branch is introduced.

## User Impact

Wizard RPC clients can now explicitly opt out of daemon installation while retaining the existing default when the field is omitted.

This lets a Companion-managed installation own service creation without changing CLI onboarding behavior.

## Evidence

- Focused `wizard.start` regression: 6/6 executions passed across the configured Vitest projects.
- Cases cover `installDaemon=false`, `true`, and omitted.
- The same test verifies `skipUi=true` and `suppressGatewayTokenOutput=true`.
- Focused `tsgo`, `oxfmt --check`, and `oxlint` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Scoped Codex Auto-review on current head returned zero findings: `patch is correct`, confidence 0.96.

Failed-first evidence was retained during development: a broad Gateway WebSocket test exceeded its inherited 90-second limit, so the PR uses a dedicated handler-level regression rather than claiming that timeout as proof. The first focused typecheck also caught a potentially absent indexed handler; the test now asserts registration before invocation.

## Scope

This PR changes only the Gateway wizard protocol projection and its focused regression test. It does not modify Windows Companion code, service defaults, packaging, migrations, or unrelated beta fixes.

The PR remains draft until the paired Windows Companion flow is validated against an official OpenClaw artifact containing this change.
